chunks: I entered upon Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), and upon him was a red sheet, new, intensely red. So I smiled when I entered, and he said: 'It is as if I know why you laughed — you laughed at this garment which is upon me. The Thaqafi woman compelled me to it, and I love her, so she compelled me to wear it.'
Then he said: 'We do not pray in this, nor should you pray in the fully saturated, blood-red dyed garment.'

He (the narrator) said: Then I entered upon him and he had already divorced her. He said: 'I heard her disavowing from Ali (peace be upon him), so there was no leeway for me to keep her while she disavows from him.'

key_terms.الثَّقَفِيَّةَ: The Thaqafi woman — a member of the Thaqif tribe; the Imam's wife at that time
key_terms.الْمُشْبَعِ الْمُضَرَّجِ: Fully saturated and blood-red dyed cloth; terms used in fiqh to specify prohibited prayer garments
key_terms.تَبَرَّأُ: To disavow, to declare religious dissociation (bara'a); in Shia doctrine, the opposite of walaya
key_terms.مِلْحَفَةٌ حَمْرَاءُ: A red sheet or outer garment; the color being the subject of the ruling

ai.seo_question: What did Imam al-Baqir say about praying in red or saturated-colored garments?
ai.summary: This narrative account describes a visit by Malik ibn A'yan to Imam al-Baqir (peace be upon him), who was wearing an intensely red garment at the insistence of his wife from the Thaqif tribe. The Imam clarified that prayer is not to be performed in fully saturated or blood-red garments, establishing a jurisprudential ruling on dress during salat. In a subsequent visit, the narrator learned the Imam had divorced his wife after hearing her disavow Imam Ali (peace be upon him) — an act of religious dissociation (bara'a) from the Imams that was utterly incompatible with continuing the marriage. This hadith touches on both dress jurisprudence and the critical importance of walaya (love and allegiance) to the Imams in Shia doctrine.
